terms.name: PIC
terms.shortDescription: Defines the format of a field
terms.longDescription: The PIC clause specifies the structure, type, and format of a field within the Data Division. It allows defining whether data is numeric, alphanumeric, decimal, signed, padded, or fixed-length. It is essential for ensuring the correct interpretation of data coming from files, screens, or batch processes.
terms.notes: The destination format controls how the value is adjusted or converted during a MOVE.

terms.name: COMP
terms.longDescription: COMP indicates that a numeric field will be stored in the hardware's native binary format. This reduces storage space and improves performance in arithmetic operations, especially in high-volume systems. Its representation depends on the hardware, requiring special attention during migration processes.
terms.notes: Ideal for intensive calculations; not suitable for data that must be exported without conversion.

terms.name: COMP-3
terms.longDescription: COMP-3 stores numbers in packed decimal format, where each digit occupies four bits and the last nibble contains the sign. It is widely used in financial applications because it maintains decimal precision without hardware dependency.
terms.notes: Prevents rounding errors typical of binary representations.

terms.name: WORKING-STORAGE
terms.longDescription: The WORKING-STORAGE section contains persistent variables throughout program execution. Counters, buffers, flags, and temporary structures are declared here. It is equivalent to static memory in modern programming languages.
terms.notes: Initial values are assigned when the program starts, not on each PERFORM.

terms.name: LINKAGE SECTION
terms.longDescription: The LINKAGE SECTION defines parameters received by the program from external sources, whether via CALL, CICS, or a calling program. It allows sharing data structures across modules.
terms.notes: Data must be mapped using USING in the PROCEDURE DIVISION.

terms.name: PROCEDURE DIVISION
terms.longDescription: The PROCEDURE DIVISION contains the executable logic of the program: calculations, validations, file reading/writing, and subprogram calls. It is organized into paragraphs and sections to improve clarity.
terms.examples:
PROCEDURE DIVISION.
    PERFORM INICIALIZAR.
    PERFORM PROCESAR-DATOS.
terms.notes: It is the core of the COBOL program.

terms.name: DATA DIVISION
terms.longDescription: The DATA DIVISION defines all the data that the program will use: files, variables, structures, and tables. It is essential for ensuring data integrity and compatibility.
terms.notes: A poor definition can cause truncation or formatting errors.

terms.name: ENVIRONMENT DIVISION
terms.longDescription: The ENVIRONMENT DIVISION describes the environment in which the program runs: file assignments, devices, and system settings. It allows adapting the program without altering its logic.
terms.notes: Crucial in batch programs that interact with physical files.

terms.name: MOVE
terms.longDescription: MOVE assigns values between fields, performing implicit conversions according to the PIC attributes of the destination. It can adjust lengths, convert types, and transform formats.
terms.examples:
MOVE 'ABC' TO CAMPO-ALFA.
MOVE 123 TO CAMPO-NUM.
terms.notes: The destination controls the conversion, not the source.

terms.name: EVALUATE
terms.longDescription: EVALUATE allows testing multiple conditions in a clear and structured manner, similar to a switch-case statement. It enhances readability and avoids nested IF statements.
terms.examples:
EVALUATE OPCION
   WHEN 'A' PERFORM ACCION-A
   WHEN 'B' PERFORM ACCION-B
   WHEN OTHER PERFORM ERROR.
terms.notes: Allows evaluating multiple expressions simultaneously.

terms.name: IF
terms.longDescription: IF enables conditional execution of code based on a logical condition. It is the core conditional structure of the language, used to validate data, control flow, and prevent errors.
terms.notes: Must be closed with END-IF to avoid ambiguities.

terms.name: CALL
terms.longDescription: CALL allows executing another program and passing parameters to it. It is fundamental for modularity and code reusability in large systems.
terms.notes: The called program must define parameters in its LINKAGE SECTION.

terms.name: FILE SECTION
terms.longDescription: The FILE SECTION defines the structure of files that the program will read or write. It includes FD descriptors and record layout structures.
terms.notes: Must correspond to the operating system or JCL definitions.

terms.name: 01 LEVEL
terms.longDescription: Level 01 defines complete data structures, such as records or group items. It represents the highest level in the COBOL data hierarchy.
terms.notes: Can contain multiple elementary sub-levels.

terms.name: 88 LEVEL
terms.longDescription: Level 88 items define symbolic conditions associated with field values, enhancing readability and avoiding explicit comparisons.
terms.notes: Does not occupy additional memory space.

terms.name: REDEFINES
terms.longDescription: REDEFINES allows interpreting the same memory block in different layout formats. It is useful for complex structures or variable data formats.
terms.examples:
01 CAMPO-A PIC X(10).
01 CAMPO-B REDEFINES CAMPO-A PIC 9(10).
terms.notes: Must be used carefully to prevent data inconsistencies.

terms.name: OCCURS
terms.longDescription: OCCURS defines tables or arrays within the Data Division, enabling structured handling of lists of items.
terms.examples:
01 TABLA.
   05 ITEM OCCURS 10 TIMES PIC X(5).
terms.notes: Can be combined with INDEXED BY for efficient table searching.

terms.name: INITIALIZE
terms.longDescription: INITIALIZE assigns default values to fields according to their data type: spaces for alphanumeric fields and zeros for numeric fields.
terms.notes: Does not affect fields defined with REDEFINES.

terms.name: STRING
terms.longDescription: STRING joins multiple strings into a destination field, offering control over positioning and delimiters.
terms.examples:
STRING NOMBRE DELIMITED BY SPACE
       APELLIDO INTO WS-NOMBRE-COMPLETO.
terms.notes: Must be used carefully to prevent buffer overflow.

terms.name: UNSTRING
terms.longDescription: UNSTRING separates a string into multiple target fields based on specified delimiters. Useful for processing variable-format data.
terms.examples: UNSTRING WS-FECHA DELIMITED BY '/' INTO DIA MES ANIO.
terms.notes: Can handle multiple delimiters simultaneously.

terms.name: INSPECT
terms.longDescription: INSPECT allows counting, replacing, or analyzing characters within a string. It is a powerful tool for data validation and sanitization.
terms.examples: INSPECT WS-TEXTO TALLYING CONTADOR FOR ALL 'A'.
terms.notes: Can be combined with REPLACING for complex string transformations.

terms.name: ACCEPT
terms.longDescription: ACCEPT retrieves data from system sources, such as current date, time, or user input.
terms.notes: Not used in CICS; replaced by environment-specific commands.

terms.name: DISPLAY
terms.longDescription: DISPLAY outputs information to the console or terminal. Useful for debugging or informational messages.
terms.notes: In CICS, it is replaced by SEND commands.

terms.name: OPEN INPUT
terms.longDescription: OPEN INPUT opens a file for sequential or random reading. It is the initial step prior to performing READ operations.
terms.notes: Must be closed with CLOSE to release system resources.

terms.name: OPEN OUTPUT
terms.longDescription: OPEN OUTPUT creates or overwrites a file for writing operations. Used before executing WRITE.
terms.notes: If the file already exists, its existing contents may be truncated.

terms.name: END-IF
terms.longDescription: END-IF explicitly terminates an IF block statement. It improves readability and eliminates ambiguity in nested conditions.
terms.notes: Required standard practice in modern COBOL code.

terms.name: END-PERFORM
terms.longDescription: END-PERFORM marks the end of an inline PERFORM block structure. It clearly delimits the code block executed within the loop, enhancing legibility and preventing scope errors.
terms.examples:
PERFORM VARYING I FROM 1 BY 1 UNTIL I > 10
    DISPLAY I
END-PERFORM.
terms.notes: Required in modern COBOL code to avoid statement ambiguity.

terms.name: END-EVALUATE
terms.longDescription: END-EVALUATE marks the end of an EVALUATE statement block. It ensures conditional branching blocks close properly while maintaining program clarity.
terms.examples:
EVALUATE OPCION
   WHEN 1 DISPLAY 'UNO'
   WHEN 2 DISPLAY 'DOS'
END-EVALUATE.
terms.notes: Prevents scoping errors when nesting multiple EVALUATE structures.

terms.name: END-READ
terms.longDescription: END-READ terminates a READ operation block. Used when the READ statement contains inline logic like AT END or NOT AT END clauses.
terms.examples:
READ ARCHIVO-IN
    AT END MOVE 'S' TO FIN
END-READ.
terms.notes: Not mandatory if the READ statement lacks conditional clause blocks.

terms.name: END-WRITE
terms.longDescription: END-WRITE marks the termination of a WRITE operation block. Used when WRITE includes additional processing logic like page advance controls.
terms.examples:
WRITE REG-OUT
    AFTER ADVANCING 1 LINE
END-WRITE.
terms.notes: Primarily used when generating printed files or report outputs.

terms.name: END-CALL
terms.longDescription: END-CALL terminates an inline CALL statement. Allows executing exception logic directly after the subprogram call within the same block.
terms.examples:
CALL 'PROG001' USING WS-DATOS
    ON EXCEPTION DISPLAY 'ERROR'
END-CALL.
terms.notes: Useful for inline error handling and checking return codes.

terms.name: END-STRING
terms.longDescription: END-STRING marks the end of an inline STRING operation. Enables incorporating conditional exception logic directly into concatenation blocks.
terms.examples:
STRING NOMBRE DELIMITED BY SPACE
       APELLIDO INTO WS-NOMBRE
END-STRING.
terms.notes: Helps avoid syntax errors when combining multiple fields.

terms.name: END-UNSTRING
terms.longDescription: END-UNSTRING marks the end of an inline UNSTRING operation block. Used when string parsing logic includes explicit conditional handling.
terms.examples:
UNSTRING WS-FECHA DELIMITED BY '/' INTO DIA MES ANIO
END-UNSTRING.
terms.notes: Useful when parsing strings containing complex delimiters.

terms.name: END-INSPECT
terms.longDescription: END-INSPECT marks the end of an inline INSPECT statement block, enabling structured transformations and character counts within a scoped block.
terms.examples:
INSPECT WS-TEXTO TALLYING CONTADOR FOR ALL 'A'
END-INSPECT.
terms.notes: Used during complex string manipulation tasks.

terms.name: SEARCH
terms.longDescription: SEARCH executes a sequential search on tables defined with OCCURS. Useful for finding elements in unsorted array structures.
terms.examples:
SEARCH TABLA
   AT END DISPLAY 'NO ENCONTRADO'
   WHEN ITEM(I) = 'X' DISPLAY 'OK'.
terms.notes: Requires the table to be defined with OCCURS and INDEXED BY.

terms.name: SEARCH ALL
terms.longDescription: SEARCH ALL executes a binary search on a sorted table, proving far more efficient than SEARCH on large datasets.
terms.examples:
SEARCH ALL TABLA
   WHEN ITEM(I) = 'X' DISPLAY 'ENCONTRADO'.
terms.notes: The underlying table must be sorted prior to executing SEARCH ALL.

terms.name: SORT
terms.longDescription: SORT reorders records from a file or table based on specified key fields. Extremely useful in batch routines requiring pre-sorted input.
terms.examples:
SORT ARCHIVO-SORT
   ON ASCENDING KEY CLAVE.
terms.notes: Can be combined with MERGE operations for complex processing pipeline needs.

terms.name: MERGE
terms.longDescription: MERGE combines multiple pre-sorted files into a single sorted file sequence. Frequently utilized in batch jobs consolidating multi-source data.
terms.examples:
MERGE ARCHIVO-A ARCHIVO-B
   ON ASCENDING KEY CLAVE
   OUTPUT PROCEDURE PROCESAR.
terms.notes: Input files must already be ordered before executing the MERGE.

terms.name: GOBACK
terms.longDescription: GOBACK passes execution control back to the invoking caller program. It acts like STOP RUN in main programs and like EXIT PROGRAM in subroutines.
terms.notes: Recommended standard in modern COBOL development due to consistent behavior across entry points.

terms.name: STOP RUN
terms.longDescription: STOP RUN completely halts program execution and closes associated environment resources. Designed for use in top-level main programs.
terms.notes: Must not be used inside called subprograms.

terms.name: USING
terms.longDescription: USING specifies parameters passed to a program from a calling module via CALL. Maps variables defined in LINKAGE SECTION with external arguments.
terms.notes: Parameter sequence must exactly match the arguments passed in the CALL statement.

terms.name: SET
terms.longDescription: SET updates index values or sets level-88 condition flags to TRUE. Useful for managing symbolic conditions and index offsets.
terms.examples:
SET ACTIVO TO TRUE.
SET I TO 1.
terms.notes: Alters logical flags or internal index values rather than performing string conversion.

terms.name: SUBTRACT
terms.longDescription: SUBTRACT performs subtraction between numeric fields. It can either modify the target value in place or store the result into a specified destination.
terms.examples:
SUBTRACT 1 FROM CONTADOR.
SUBTRACT A B FROM C.
terms.notes: Care must be taken to prevent arithmetic underflow or size errors in small fields.

terms.name: IDENTIFICATION DIVISION
terms.longDescription: The IDENTIFICATION DIVISION specifies program metadata and header information. It contains statements such as PROGRAM-ID, AUTHOR, DATE-WRITTEN, and REMARKS, acting as the declarative entry point for the source module.
terms.notes: Must be the very first division in every COBOL source file.

terms.name: PROGRAM-ID
terms.longDescription: PROGRAM-ID declares the unique identifier for the COBOL program. This name is referenced during CALL statements and compiler linkage. Must be alphanumeric with no spaces.
terms.notes: The name should match the source module or generated executable name.

terms.name: CONFIGURATION SECTION
terms.longDescription: The CONFIGURATION SECTION within the ENVIRONMENT DIVISION specifies compile-time and runtime settings, such as character sets, collating sequences, and physical devices. Helps adapt programs across platforms.
terms.examples:
CONFIGURATION SECTION.
SOURCE-COMPUTER. IBM-3270.
OBJECT-COMPUTER. IBM-3270.
terms.notes: Optional in modern compilers, but useful for cross-system portability.

terms.name: INPUT-OUTPUT SECTION
terms.longDescription: The INPUT-OUTPUT SECTION specifies physical files and external devices used by the program. Contains FILE-CONTROL and I-O-CONTROL clauses describing physical file assignments and organizations.
terms.examples:
INPUT-OUTPUT SECTION.
FILE-CONTROL.
    SELECT ARCHIVO-IN ASSIGN TO 'ENTRADA.DAT'.
terms.notes: Must precede the FILE SECTION located in the DATA DIVISION.

terms.name: COMPUTE
terms.longDescription: COMPUTE allows evaluating multi-operator mathematical expressions in a single statement, including addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and parenthesized operations.
terms.notes: Target variable must be numeric and sized to hold the calculated expression result.

terms.name: ADD
terms.longDescription: ADD executes addition across numeric fields. It can update target fields directly or output results into a destination field using GIVING, accepting multiple operands.
terms.examples:
ADD 5 TO CONTADOR.
ADD A B TO TOTAL.
terms.notes: Ensure destination field size avoids numeric overflow errors.

terms.name: MULTIPLY
terms.longDescription: MULTIPLY performs multiplication on numeric data fields. Results can update the original field or be stored into a target field. Useful for computing totals and ratios.
terms.examples: MULTIPLY PRECIO BY CANTIDAD GIVING IMPORTE.
terms.notes: Destination size must accommodate maximum potential product value to prevent truncation.

terms.name: DIVIDE
terms.longDescription: DIVIDE executes division between numeric fields. It supports returning quotients and remainders via the GIVING and REMAINDER clauses.
terms.examples: DIVIDE TOTAL BY 10 GIVING PROMEDIO REMAINDER RESTO.
terms.notes: Logic must guard against divide-by-zero runtime exceptions.

terms.name: CURRENT-DATE
terms.shortDescription: Gets current system date and time
terms.longDescription: CURRENT-DATE returns system timestamp details in YYYYMMDDHHMMSSCC format. Frequently used for auditing, logging, and time-stamped calculations.
terms.notes: Requires an alphanumeric receiver field long enough to contain the complete timestamp string.

terms.name: IF Statement Nesting
terms.longDescription: Nesting IF statements permits evaluating complex multi-level decision logic. Used when logic requires evaluating dependent conditional trees. Requires careful formatting to maintain readability.
terms.examples:
IF A > 0
    IF B = 'S'
        PERFORM PROCESAR
    END-IF
END-IF.
terms.notes: Replacing deep nesting with EVALUATE statements is recommended for clarity.

terms.name: PERFORM
terms.shortDescription: Executes code blocks, paragraphs, or sections as routines
terms.longDescription: PERFORM invokes paragraphs or sections within the PROCEDURE DIVISION. It serves as the primary mechanism for modular logic and loop control, reducing code duplication and easing maintenance. Can be run simply, as a loop, or with inline parameters.
terms.examples:
PERFORM INICIALIZAR.
PERFORM PROCESAR-DATOS UNTIL FIN = 'S'.
PERFORM VARYING I FROM 1 BY 1 UNTIL I > 10.
terms.notes: The target paragraph or section must exist in the program structure.

terms.name: EXIT
terms.longDescription: EXIT provides an exit point from a paragraph or section without stopping program execution. Helps manage execution path flow inside the PROCEDURE DIVISION.
terms.notes: Do not confuse with EXIT PROGRAM, which exits the subprogram module entirely.

terms.name: STOP
terms.longDescription: STOP pauses program execution at designated points, typically for manual operator control or debugging. Unlike STOP RUN, it does not close the runtime execution state.
terms.notes: Rarely used in production systems; primarily used during development testing.

terms.name: EXAMINE
terms.longDescription: EXAMINE is a legacy statement used to search and replace character strings. Replaced by INSPECT in modern COBOL, though still encountered in legacy applications.
terms.notes: Obsolete; INSPECT is the modern standard replacement.

terms.name: TRANSFORM
terms.shortDescription: Transforms characters based on a mapping table
terms.longDescription: TRANSFORM converts character strings according to a user-defined mapping table. Useful for character translation or data normalization tasks.
terms.examples: TRANSFORM WS-CADENA FROM TABLA-ORIGEN TO TABLA-DESTINO.
terms.notes: Transformation source and target lookup tables must be properly defined.

terms.name: COMPILE
terms.longDescription: COMPILE refers to the build process translating COBOL source code into object code or executable modules. Involves syntax parsing, division validation, and target code generation.
terms.notes: Specific command syntax depends on compiler environment (e.g., IBM, Micro Focus, GnuCOBOL).

terms.name: DEPENDING ON
terms.shortDescription: Controls variable length in OCCURS clauses
terms.longDescription: DEPENDING ON defines variable-length arrays within OCCURS clauses. The active element count is dynamically determined at runtime based on a field value.
terms.examples: 05 ITEMS OCCURS 1 TO 50 DEPENDING ON WS-CANTIDAD PIC X(10).
terms.notes: The control field specified in DEPENDING ON must contain a valid numeric value.

terms.name: USAGE INDEX
terms.shortDescription: Defines index data items for tables
terms.longDescription: USAGE INDEX specifies that a field acts as a table index for OCCURS arrays, enabling optimized binary and sequential lookup handling via SEARCH statements.
terms.notes: Index items hold internal byte displacements rather than ordinal position numbers.

terms.name: FILE-CONTROL
terms.longDescription: FILE-CONTROL maps logical program file names to external physical devices or files. Includes SELECT, ASSIGN, ORGANIZATION, ACCESS MODE, and FILE STATUS clauses.
terms.notes: Must be located in the INPUT-OUTPUT SECTION.

terms.name: ASSIGN
terms.shortDescription: Binds a logical file to a physical destination
terms.longDescription: ASSIGN maps a COBOL logical file identifier to an operating system file path, DDNAME, or device.
terms.notes: Exact syntax varies across platforms (z/OS, UNIX, Windows).

terms.name: ORGANIZATION
terms.longDescription: The ORGANIZATION clause specifies record arrangement inside physical files: SEQUENTIAL, RELATIVE, or INDEXED. It dictates permitted file access methods and storage management.
terms.examples:
SELECT ARCHIVO ASSIGN TO 'DATOS.DAT'
    ORGANIZATION IS SEQUENTIAL.
terms.notes: Must remain consistent with FD definition and access specifications.

terms.name: ACCESS
terms.longDescription: ACCESS MODE specifies record read/write operations mode: SEQUENTIAL, RANDOM, or DYNAMIC. It controls how the program interacts with file record pointers.
terms.examples:
SELECT ARCHIVO ASSIGN TO 'DATOS.DAT'
    ACCESS MODE IS DYNAMIC.
terms.notes: Must align with the specified file ORGANIZATION mode.

terms.name: LOCK
terms.longDescription: LOCK specifies record locking behavior in indexed or relative files. It prevents concurrent access that could cause data inconsistencies.
terms.notes: Usage depends on the environment (CICS, batch, VSAM).

terms.name: RECORD KEY
terms.longDescription: RECORD KEY defines the field that acts as the primary key in indexed files, enabling efficient record lookup.
terms.notes: Must be defined in the FILE SECTION with a compatible PIC.

terms.name: FILE STATUS
terms.longDescription: FILE STATUS specifies a field where the system stores the result of each file operation, allowing detection of errors such as end-of-file, missing records, or access issues.
terms.notes: Must be checked after every READ, WRITE, or REWRITE operation.

terms.name: I-O CONTROL
terms.longDescription: I-O CONTROL defines advanced file management options such as buffering, synchronization, and device control, typically used in high-performance batch systems.
terms.notes: Rarely used in modern compilers.

terms.name: FD
terms.shortDescription: File descriptor in the DATA DIVISION.
terms.longDescription: FD defines the characteristics of the physical file structure, including record length, format, access mode, and fields. It is essential for READ, WRITE, REWRITE, and DELETE operations.
terms.notes: Must correspond with the definition in FILE-CONTROL and be associated with a SELECT in the ENVIRONMENT DIVISION.

terms.name: LABEL RECORD
terms.longDescription: LABEL RECORD specifies whether a file contains standard or omitted labels, used in environments where physical files include header metadata.
terms.notes: Relevant in traditional mainframe environments.

terms.name: VALUE OF FILE-ID
terms.longDescription: VALUE OF FILE-ID specifies the physical filename in the operating system as an alternative to ASSIGN.
terms.notes: Not all compilers support this clause.

terms.name: RECORDING MODE
terms.longDescription: RECORDING MODE defines how records are stored in the file: F (fixed), V (variable), or U (undefined), controlling the physical file structure.
terms.notes: Must be consistent with record lengths.

terms.name: BLOCK CONTAINS
terms.shortDescription: Defines the physical block size of the file.
terms.longDescription: BLOCK CONTAINS specifies the number of records comprising a physical block within the file, used to optimize read and write operations in block-structured storage.
terms.notes: Must be consistent with RECORDING MODE and record lengths.

terms.name: RECORD CONTAINS
terms.longDescription: RECORD CONTAINS specifies the minimum and maximum length of file records, essential for variable-length files and data integrity.
terms.notes: Must match the structure defined in the FD.

terms.name: DATA RECORD
terms.shortDescription: Associates logical records to the file.
terms.longDescription: DATA RECORD specifies the names of the records defined in the FILE SECTION that belong to the file, linking multiple record structures to a single FD.
terms.notes: Must reference names defined in the FILE SECTION.

terms.name: LINAGE
terms.longDescription: LINAGE defines the number of lines per page for files destined for printing, managing headers, footers, and automatic page breaks.
terms.notes: Used primarily in reports and printed listings.

terms.name: CODE-SET
terms.longDescription: CODE-SET specifies the encoding used to store file characters, such as ASCII or EBCDIC, ensuring compatibility across systems.
terms.notes: Must be compatible with the execution environment.

terms.name: VALUE
terms.shortDescription: Defines initial values in file definitions.
terms.longDescription: VALUE specifies default values for certain file attributes, used in environments where files require initial metadata.
terms.notes: Not all compilers implement this clause.

terms.name: Sequential file
terms.shortDescription: File with records in sequential physical order.
terms.longDescription: A sequential file stores records in consecutive physical order. It only allows sequential access, making it suitable for batch processing and full file traversals.
terms.notes: Random access is not permitted.

terms.name: SELECT for sequential files
terms.longDescription: SELECT defines the logical assignment of a sequential file, indicating its physical path and organization as a first step for file handling in COBOL.
terms.examples:
SELECT ARCHIVO-IN ASSIGN TO 'ENTRADA.DAT'
    ORGANIZATION IS SEQUENTIAL.
terms.notes: Must be supplemented with an FD in the DATA DIVISION.

terms.name: OPEN
terms.shortDescription: Opens a file for reading or writing.
terms.longDescription: OPEN prepares a file for input or output operations. It can open in INPUT, OUTPUT, I-O, or EXTEND mode depending on the required operation.
terms.notes: Must be closed with CLOSE to release resources.

terms.name: WRITE
terms.shortDescription: Writes a record to a file.
terms.longDescription: WRITE writes a record to a sequential, relative, or indexed file. It can include page advance control for printed files and additional options depending on file organization.
terms.notes: The file must be open in OUTPUT, I-O, or EXTEND mode.

terms.name: CLOSE
terms.shortDescription: Closes a file and releases resources.
terms.longDescription: CLOSE finalizes access to a file and releases associated resources. It is mandatory to prevent locks, inconsistencies, and ensure data integrity.
terms.notes: Must be executed before program termination or changing access modes.

terms.name: READ
terms.shortDescription: Reads a record from a file.
terms.longDescription: READ retrieves a record from a sequential, relative, or indexed file. It can include AT END or INVALID KEY clauses to handle special conditions.
terms.examples: READ ARCHIVO-IN AT END MOVE 'S' TO FIN.
terms.notes: AT END or INVALID KEY must be handled to prevent read errors.

terms.name: REWRITE
terms.longDescription: REWRITE updates a previously read record in relative or indexed files. It requires the record to have been read first using READ.
terms.notes: Not available for sequential files.

terms.name: START
terms.shortDescription: Positions an indexed or relative file.
terms.longDescription: START positions the file pointer at a specific record based on the key, allowing sequential READ operations to begin from a determined position.
terms.notes: Only valid for indexed or relative files.

terms.name: DELETE
terms.shortDescription: Deletes a record from a file.
terms.longDescription: DELETE removes a record from relative or indexed files. It requires the record to have been previously located via READ.
terms.notes: Not available for sequential files.

terms.name: Relative files
terms.longDescription: Relative files allow access to records via their relative number. They support sequential, random, and dynamic access, making them suitable for structures with fixed positions.
terms.notes: Require a RELATIVE KEY field for READ and REWRITE operations.

terms.name: File matching
terms.longDescription: File matching consists of comparing records from two or more sorted files to detect matches, differences, or generate consolidations. Common in integration batch processes.
terms.notes: Files must be sorted by the same key.

terms.name: Matching
terms.longDescription: Matching is the technique of traversing sequential files in parallel to compare keys and process matches or discrepancies, used in reconciliations and integration processes.
terms.notes: Requires end-of-file control on each file.

terms.name: PROGRAM COMMUNICATION
terms.longDescription: Program communication allows a COBOL module to invoke another and share data structures using CALL, LINKAGE SECTION, and USING, essential for modular and layered architectures.
terms.notes: Parameters must match in order and format.

terms.name: Routine
terms.shortDescription: Reusable code block within the program.
terms.longDescription: A routine is a paragraph or section inside the PROCEDURE DIVISION that encapsulates specific logic. It is invoked via PERFORM and structures the program into clear functional units.
terms.notes: Must be clearly identified to facilitate maintenance.

terms.name: ENTRY
terms.longDescription: ENTRY defines additional entry points within a COBOL program, allowing it to be invoked from different contexts or with different parameters. Used in complex modules requiring multiple interfaces.
terms.notes: Must be located after the PROCEDURE DIVISION.

terms.name: EXIT PROGRAM
terms.shortDescription: Ends the program and returns to caller.
terms.longDescription: EXIT PROGRAM ends the execution of the current program and returns control to the calling program, equivalent to a clean return in subprograms.
terms.notes: Does not terminate the entire environment; only the current module.

terms.name: CANCEL
terms.longDescription: CANCEL removes a program previously loaded via CALL, forcing the next invocation to reload it from the system, used when a module's state needs re-initialization.
terms.notes: Useful when the program maintains internal state that must be reset.

terms.name: CHAIN
terms.shortDescription: Transfers control to another program without return.
terms.longDescription: CHAIN transfers execution to another program, passing parameters without the possibility of returning to the original program, useful in flows where the initial module should not continue.
terms.notes: Not all compilers implement this statement.

terms.name: RETURN-CODE
terms.longDescription: RETURN-CODE is a special variable indicating program execution results, used to communicate states to upper programs, control scripts, or operating systems.
terms.notes: Must be carefully managed in batch processes.

terms.name: JOB
terms.shortDescription: Starts a batch job in z/OS
terms.longDescription: The JOB statement marks the beginning of a batch job in z/OS. It defines global parameters such as the user, execution class, message level, and time limit. It serves as the entry point for any batch process and controls how the JES2/JES3 system manages the job.
terms.notes: Must be the first statement in the JCL. Parameters depend on the JES environment.

terms.name: EXEC
terms.longDescription: EXEC indicates that a step will execute a program or a procedure stored in a PROCLIB. It is the core of each job step, defining which program runs and with what parameters.
terms.notes: If a PROC is used, parameters are passed via PARM or symbolic variables.

terms.name: DD
terms.longDescription: DD (Data Definition) specifies datasets, files, queues, or resources required by a program. It defines the logical name, location, space, format, and disposition of the dataset.
terms.notes: Each EXEC can have multiple associated DD statements.

terms.name: STEPLIB
terms.shortDescription: Load library for a single step
terms.longDescription: STEPLIB defines a specific load library for a single step. It allows the program to execute using modules from a library other than the standard system libraries.
terms.notes: Only affects the step where it is declared.

terms.name: JOBLIB
terms.shortDescription: Load library for the entire job
terms.longDescription: JOBLIB defines a load library for all steps in the job. It is useful when multiple programs require the same custom library.
terms.notes: Must be placed immediately after the JOB statement.

terms.name: SYSOUT
terms.longDescription: SYSOUT defines the output class for messages generated by the system or the program. It routes output to print queues or logs depending on the configuration.
terms.notes: The class determines where the output will be sent.

terms.name: SYSPRINT
terms.longDescription: SYSPRINT captures the print output generated by the program. It is commonly used with utilities such as IDCAMS, IEBGENER, or SORT.
terms.notes: Generally used alongside SYSIN.

terms.name: SYSIN
terms.longDescription: SYSIN provides direct input to the program, typically parameters or control statements. It is essential for utilities that require internal commands.
terms.notes: Can use inline data or reference a dataset.

terms.name: DISP
terms.longDescription: DISP controls the dataset status: creation, exclusive use, shared use, and the action to take when the step ends. It is critical for avoiding locks and data loss.
terms.notes: The first parameter is the initial status; the second and third are post-execution actions.

terms.name: DSN
terms.longDescription: DSN specifies the fully qualified name of the dataset. It can be sequential, VSAM, or a PDS member.
terms.notes: Names must follow the HLQ.MLQ.LLQ convention.

terms.name: SPACE
terms.longDescription: SPACE defines the amount of space allocated to a dataset. It can be specified in cylinders, tracks, or blocks.
terms.notes: The first value is the primary allocation; the second is the secondary extent.

terms.name: UNIT
terms.longDescription: UNIT indicates the type of device where the dataset will be stored. SYSDA is the most common for disk storage.
terms.notes: UNIT=TAPE is used for magnetic tapes.

terms.name: VOL
terms.shortDescription: Physical volume where the dataset resides
terms.longDescription: VOL specifies the physical volume where the dataset is located or will be created. It is useful for datasets on specific tapes or disks.
terms.notes: Not always necessary; the system catalog can resolve it.

terms.name: DCB
terms.longDescription: DCB defines dataset attributes such as record format, length, and block size. It is essential for sequential datasets.
terms.notes: Can be omitted if the dataset is already cataloged.

terms.name: RECFM
terms.longDescription: RECFM defines the record format: fixed (FB), variable (VB), fixed blocked (FBS), or variable blocked (VBS).
terms.notes: FB is the most common format for text files.

terms.name: LRECL
terms.longDescription: LRECL indicates the length of each record in bytes. It is mandatory for FB files.
terms.notes: Must match the format expected by the processing program.

terms.name: BLKSIZE
terms.longDescription: BLKSIZE defines the physical block size on disk. An appropriate value improves performance.
terms.notes: If omitted, the system can calculate it automatically.

terms.name: MSGCLASS
terms.longDescription: MSGCLASS determines the output queue where job log messages will be sent. Each class has a different destination based on system configuration.
terms.notes: Classes depend on the JES environment.

terms.name: CLASS
terms.longDescription: CLASS defines the priority and execution type of the job. Jobs with a higher priority class may run sooner.
terms.notes: Classes are defined by the system administrator.

terms.name: TYPRUN
terms.longDescription: TYPRUN allows executing the job in a special mode: SCAN validates the JCL without executing it; HOLD retains the job in the input queue.
terms.notes: Useful for validating JCL before production deployment.

terms.name: COND
terms.longDescription: COND controls whether a step should execute based on the return codes of preceding steps. It helps avoid unnecessary executions.
terms.notes: Logic can become complex; simplification is recommended.

terms.name: RC
terms.longDescription: RC is the return code generated by a program, indicating success, warnings, or errors.
terms.notes: Common standard values are 0, 4, 8, 12, and 16.

terms.name: ABEND
terms.longDescription: ABEND indicates that a job or program terminated abnormally, which can be caused by JCL errors, logic bugs, or resource issues.
terms.notes: Core dumps assist in diagnosing the underlying issue.

terms.name: PROC
terms.longDescription: PROC defines a reusable procedure stored in a PROCLIB library, allowing common job steps to be standardized.
terms.notes: Parameters are passed using symbolic variables.

terms.name: PEND
terms.longDescription: PEND marks the end of a PROC definition, which is required to properly close the procedure block.
terms.notes: Must be the last line of the PROC.

terms.name: INCLUDE
terms.longDescription: INCLUDE allows inserting content from another PDS member directly into the JCL stream, facilitating the reuse of common snippets.
terms.notes: The member must reside in a system-defined procedure library.

terms.name: SET
terms.longDescription: SET assigns values to symbolic variables used within PROCs or JCL streams, enabling parameterized executions.
terms.notes: Variables are referenced using &DATE syntax.

terms.name: SYMBOLIC
terms.longDescription: Symbolic variables allow parameterizing procedures, with values substituted at execution time.
terms.notes: Defined within a PROC statement or via SET.

terms.name: IEFBR14
terms.shortDescription: Null program used to create/delete datasets
terms.longDescription: IEFBR14 is an empty dummy program that always returns RC=0. It is used to execute DD statements that create or delete datasets without extra logic.
terms.notes: Widely used for housekeeping tasks.

terms.name: IDCAMS
terms.longDescription: IDCAMS manages VSAM datasets, catalogs, and operations such as DELETE, DEFINE, REPRO, and LISTCAT.
terms.notes: One of the most powerful storage management utilities in the system.

terms.name: IEBGENER
terms.longDescription: IEBGENER copies sequential datasets, prints file contents, or generates simple reports. It is a versatile utility for basic file manipulation.
terms.notes: Can copy PDS members, sequential datasets, and SYSOUT streams.

terms.name: IEBCOPY
terms.longDescription: IEBCOPY copies, compresses, and reorganizes PDS members, making it essential for library maintenance.
terms.notes: Allows copying multiple members simultaneously.

terms.name: SORT
terms.longDescription: SORT is one of the most widely used utilities in z/OS. It sorts, filters, summarizes, and transforms sequential datasets. Its power lies in defining multiple keys, conditions, and complex operations without writing custom programs.
terms.notes: Handles massive files and supports numerous advanced data manipulation operations.

terms.name: ICETOOL
terms.longDescription: ICETOOL is a high-level interface to DFSORT that performs complex operations such as statistics, validations, reporting, conditional copying, and advanced transformations. It simplifies tasks that would require multiple SORT steps.
terms.notes: Ideal for batch processes requiring deep data analysis and custom reporting.

terms.name: SYSUDUMP
terms.longDescription: SYSUDUMP generates a formatted memory dump when an abend occurs. It includes program info, registers, and storage contents useful for diagnostics.
terms.notes: Produces a human-readable dump format.

terms.name: SYSABEND
terms.longDescription: SYSABEND generates a more detailed dump than SYSUDUMP, including additional system control blocks and execution environment data.
terms.notes: Useful for deep failure analysis.

terms.name: SYSMDUMP
terms.longDescription: SYSMDUMP produces a compact, machine-formatted dump oriented toward automated analysis tools. It is the most detailed of the three core dump types.
terms.notes: Requires specialized tools to interpret.

terms.name: TIME
terms.longDescription: TIME defines the maximum execution time allowed for a job or step, preventing defective processes from consuming system resources indefinitely.
terms.notes: 1440 indicates unlimited execution time.

terms.name: REGION
terms.longDescription: REGION specifies the amount of memory available to the job or step. It is crucial for programs requiring large buffers or intensive processing.
terms.notes: 0M allows the system to assign the maximum available memory.

terms.name: NOTIFY
terms.longDescription: NOTIFY indicates which user will receive a message when the job finishes, helping monitor long-running or critical executions.
terms.notes: SYSUID refers to the user who submitted the job.

terms.name: MSGLEVEL
terms.longDescription: MSGLEVEL controls which messages appear in the job log output, helping reduce clutter or increase diagnostic detail as needed.
terms.notes: The first value controls system messages; the second controls job-related messages.

terms.name: PARM
terms.longDescription: PARM sends parameters directly to the program executed in the step, allowing behavior to be controlled without modifying code.
terms.notes: The target program must be designed to receive them.

terms.name: DDNAME
terms.longDescription: DDNAME is the logical identifier a program uses to reference a dataset. Each DD has a unique name within the step.
terms.notes: Must match the name expected by the program.

terms.name: CATALOG
terms.shortDescription: Registers a dataset in the system catalog
terms.longDescription: CATALOG registers a dataset in the system catalog, enabling it to be located later without specifying a physical volume serial.
terms.notes: IDCAMS manages the majority of catalog operations.

terms.name: UNCATALOG
terms.shortDescription: Removes a dataset from the catalog
terms.longDescription: UNCATALOG removes the dataset entry from the catalog without necessarily deleting the physical dataset itself.
terms.notes: May require VOL=SER if the dataset continues to exist physically.

terms.name: DELETE
terms.longDescription: DELETE erases a dataset from the system, commonly used for housekeeping or cleanup of temporary files.
terms.notes: IDCAMS is the most common utility for this operation.

terms.name: ALLOCATE
terms.longDescription: ALLOCATE creates a dataset by specifying space, format, and attributes, which is useful for preparing files ahead of batch processing.
terms.notes: Can be replaced by IEFBR14 with a NEW DD statement.

terms.name: FREE
terms.longDescription: FREE releases a previously allocated dataset, avoiding locks or freeing up system resources.
terms.notes: Does not delete the dataset; only releases the allocation.

terms.name: PRINT
terms.longDescription: PRINT prints the content of a dataset, typically utilizing utilities like IEBGENER or SORT.
terms.notes: Useful for quick file inspection.

terms.name: COPY
terms.longDescription: COPY copies entire datasets or PDS members, a common operation in library maintenance tasks.
terms.notes: IEBCOPY is the most widely used utility for copying PDS libraries.

terms.name: TRANID
terms.longDescription: TRANID is the four-character identifier representing the executing CICS transaction. It determines which program is invoked and how the user session behaves, playing a vital role in routing requests within interactive environments.
terms.notes: Must be defined in the CSD and enabled using CEDA.

terms.name: COMMAREA
terms.longDescription: COMMAREA is a memory block used to pass data between CICS programs via LINK, XCTL, or RETURN. It maintains state across screens and modules, making it essential for transactional applications.
terms.examples: EXEC CICS LINK PROGRAM('PROG2') COMMAREA(WS-DATA) END-EXEC
terms.notes: Its length is indicated in EIBCALEN.

terms.name: MAPSET
terms.longDescription: A MAPSET is a collection of screens defined using BMS. It groups multiple maps that form part of a single user interface, facilitating screen organization and reuse.
terms.notes: Must be loaded in the system map library.

terms.name: MAP
terms.longDescription: A MAP is an individual screen within a MAPSET. It defines fields, positions, attributes, and visual behavior on 3270 terminals.
terms.notes: Each MAP can contain multiple DFHMDF field definitions.

terms.name: EXEC CICS SEND
terms.shortDescription: Sends a screen to the terminal
terms.longDescription: SEND transmits a map or text to a 3270 terminal. It is the primary instruction for displaying information to users in CICS applications.
terms.examples: EXEC CICS SEND MAP('MENU') MAPSET('MENUSET') END-EXEC
terms.notes: Can include CURSOR, ERASE, and other formatting options.

terms.name: EXEC CICS RECEIVE
terms.longDescription: RECEIVE retrieves data entered by the user on a previously sent screen, making it essential for processing forms and user input.
terms.examples: EXEC CICS RECEIVE MAP('MENU') INTO(WS-MENU) END-EXEC
terms.notes: Must handle AID indicators to identify the pressed key.

terms.name: EXEC CICS LINK
terms.longDescription: LINK invokes another CICS program and returns control to the calling program, enabling modularity and logic reuse.
terms.examples: EXEC CICS LINK PROGRAM('PROG2') COMMAREA(WS-DATA) END-EXEC
terms.notes: The called program must define DFHCOMMAREA.

terms.name: EXEC CICS XCTL
terms.longDescription: XCTL transfers control to another program without returning to the caller. It is useful for completely changing the execution flow.
terms.examples: EXEC CICS XCTL PROGRAM('MENU') COMMAREA(WS-DATA) END-EXEC
terms.notes: The calling program does not regain control.

terms.name: EXEC CICS RETURN
terms.longDescription: RETURN ends execution of the current program and returns control to the calling program or terminal. It can pass a COMMAREA.
terms.notes: Can include TRANSID to initiate another transaction.

terms.name: EIBCALEN
terms.longDescription: EIBCALEN contains the length of the COMMAREA received by the program, allowing validation of whether data was passed correctly.
terms.examples: IF EIBCALEN = 0 THEN MOVE 'S' TO WS-NO-DATA
terms.notes: If zero, no COMMAREA was received.

terms.name: EIBTRNID
terms.longDescription: EIBTRNID contains the identifier of the transaction executing the program, useful for auditing and flow control.
terms.notes: Always exactly 4 characters long.

terms.name: EIBTIME
terms.longDescription: EIBTIME contains the time the transaction started, used for auditing and performance measurement.
terms.notes: Formatted as HHMMSS.

terms.name: EIBDATE
terms.longDescription: EIBDATE contains the date the transaction started, useful for traceability.
terms.notes: Formatted as YYDDD (Julian date).

terms.name: DFHCOMMAREA
terms.longDescription: DFHCOMMAREA is the standard structure where data is received and sent between CICS programs. It must be declared in WORKING-STORAGE.
terms.notes: Must match the length sent in LINK/XCTL.

terms.name: TS QUEUE
terms.longDescription: TS queues allow storing data temporarily during transaction execution, useful for processes requiring short persistence.
terms.examples: EXEC CICS WRITEQ TS QUEUE('TEMP1') FROM(WS-DATA) END-EXEC
terms.notes: Automatically deleted when the task ends.

terms.name: TD QUEUE
terms.longDescription: TD queues allow sending data to external destinations such as printers or logs. They are persistent and processed outside the transaction.
terms.examples: EXEC CICS WRITEQ TD QUEUE('PRT1') FROM(WS-LINE) END-EXEC
terms.notes: TD queues can be internal or external.

terms.name: EXEC CICS READQ TS
terms.longDescription: READQ TS reads data previously stored in a TS queue, used to retrieve information across transaction steps.
terms.examples: EXEC CICS READQ TS QUEUE('TEMP1') INTO(WS-DATA) END-EXEC
terms.notes: Must handle ITEMERR if the queue is empty.

terms.name: EXEC CICS WRITEQ TS
terms.shortDescription: Writes to a temporary storage queue
terms.longDescription: WRITEQ TS stores data temporarily in a TS queue, useful for keeping information between screens.
terms.examples: EXEC CICS WRITEQ TS QUEUE('TEMP1') FROM(WS-DATA) END-EXEC
terms.notes: TS queues are task-specific.

terms.name: EXEC CICS READQ TD
terms.longDescription: READQ TD reads data from a TD queue, typically processed by external subsystems like printers or logs.
terms.examples: EXEC CICS READQ TD QUEUE('PRT1') INTO(WS-LINE) END-EXEC
terms.notes: TD queues can be internal or external.

terms.name: EXEC CICS WRITEQ TD
terms.shortDescription: Writes to a transient data queue
terms.longDescription: WRITEQ TD sends data to a TD queue to be processed outside the transaction. Common for printing or auditing.
terms.examples: EXEC CICS WRITEQ TD QUEUE('PRT1') FROM(WS-LINE) END-EXEC
terms.notes: External TD queues may require additional setup.

terms.name: HANDLE CONDITION
terms.longDescription: HANDLE CONDITION captures specific errors like NOTFND, PGMIDERR, or MAPFAIL, essential for controlling failures without abends.
terms.examples: EXEC CICS HANDLE CONDITION NOTFND(PROC-NF) END-EXEC
terms.notes: Must be declared before the instruction that might fail.

terms.name: HANDLE AID
terms.longDescription: HANDLE AID captures function keys such as PF1–PF24 or PA1–PA3, essential for navigating CICS screens.
terms.examples: EXEC CICS HANDLE AID PF3(PROC-EXIT) END-EXEC
terms.notes: Must be declared before a RECEIVE statement.

terms.name: AID
terms.longDescription: AID contains the code of the key pressed by the user, such as PF3, PF5, ENTER, or CLEAR, enabling navigation control.
terms.examples: IF EIBAID = DFHPF3 THEN PERFORM EXIT
terms.notes: EIBAID holds the value of the last pressed attention identifier.

terms.name: PF KEY
terms.longDescription: PF keys are 3270 terminal function keys that allow quick execution of actions such as exiting, scrolling back, or confirming.
terms.notes: Used in combination with HANDLE AID or EIBAID checks.

terms.name: PA KEY
terms.longDescription: PA Keys are special keys that send immediate attention to the system without transmitting screen data.
terms.notes: Used for administrative functions.

terms.name: BMS
terms.longDescription: BMS is the CICS system for defining screens using MAPSETs and MAPs. It allows control of fields, attributes, and positions on 3270 terminals.
terms.notes: Generates assembler macros and COBOL copybooks.

terms.name: DFHMSD
terms.longDescription: DFHMSD defines a MAPSET, grouping one or more MAPs. It includes global attributes such as type, name, and generation options.
terms.notes: Must contain one or more DFHMDI.

terms.name: DFHMDI
terms.longDescription: DFHMDI defines a MAP within a MAPSET. It establishes the MAP name and its general characteristics.
terms.notes: Must contain one or more DFHMDF.

terms.name: DFHMDF
terms.longDescription: DFHMDF defines a field within a MAP, specifying position, length, attributes, and behavior.
terms.notes: It is the basic element of a BMS screen.

terms.name: ATTRB
terms.longDescription: ATTRB defines the visual and functional attributes of a field, such as BRIGHT, DARK, PROT, UNPROT, FSET, IC, ASKIP.
terms.notes: Controls how the user interacts with the field.

terms.name: PROT
terms.longDescription: PROT indicates that the field cannot be modified by the user. It is useful for labels or fixed information.
terms.notes: The cursor cannot be placed on PROT fields.

terms.name: UNPROT
terms.longDescription: UNPROT indicates that the field is editable by the user. It is the most common attribute in CICS forms.
terms.notes: Must be combined with FSET if the field always needs to be sent.

terms.name: BRIGHT
terms.longDescription: BRIGHT is a BMS attribute that displays the field in high intensity, visually highlighting it on the terminal screen. It is used to emphasize important information or guide the user during interaction.
terms.notes: The attribute depends on 3270 terminal support.

terms.name: DARK
terms.longDescription: DARK is the BMS attribute that displays the field in normal intensity. It is the default value for most fields on CICS screens.
terms.notes: Used for standard text that does not require emphasis.

terms.name: ASKIP
terms.longDescription: ASKIP indicates that the field cannot be selected or modified by the user. It is useful for displaying fixed information or labels on the screen.
terms.notes: The cursor cannot be placed on ASKIP fields.

terms.name: FSET
terms.longDescription: FSET marks the field as modified, even if the user has not changed it. This forces CICS to send the field content to the program during a RECEIVE.
terms.notes: Very useful for fields that must always be sent to the program.

terms.name: IC
terms.longDescription: IC (Initial Cursor) automatically places the cursor in the specified field when the screen is sent. It improves user experience by guiding data entry.
terms.notes: Only one field should have IC per screen.

terms.name: CURSOR
terms.longDescription: CURSOR allows specifying the exact position of the cursor on the screen during a SEND. It is useful for controlling user interaction on dynamic screens.
terms.examples: EXEC CICS SEND MAP('MENU') CURSOR(120) END-EXEC
terms.notes: The position is indicated in linear coordinates of the 3270 buffer.

terms.name: SYNCPOINT
terms.longDescription: SYNCPOINT commits all updates made by the transaction, ensuring integrity in databases and queues. It is equivalent to a COMMIT in transactional systems.
terms.notes: Mandatory in processes that update VSAM or DB2.

terms.name: ROLLBACK
terms.longDescription: ROLLBACK reverses all updates made by the transaction since the last SYNCPOINT. It is used to handle errors and maintain data integrity.
terms.notes: Only rolls back transactional changes, not sent screens.

terms.name: ENQ
terms.longDescription: ENQ locks a resource to prevent simultaneous access by other transactions. It is useful for protecting records or files during critical updates.
terms.notes: Must be released with DEQ to avoid prolonged lockouts.

terms.name: DEQ
terms.longDescription: DEQ releases a resource previously locked with ENQ, allowing other transactions to access it.
terms.notes: Must always be executed to avoid deadlocks.

terms.name: PROGRAM
terms.longDescription: PROGRAM identifies a COBOL or assembler module registered in CICS for execution. It must be defined in the CSD (CICS System Definition).
terms.notes: Must be enabled via CEDA or DFHCSDUP.

terms.name: TRANSACTION
terms.longDescription: TRANSACTION is the four-character identifier that starts the execution of a CICS program. It is defined in the CSD and associated with a PROGRAM.
terms.notes: Must be enabled to be executed from a terminal.

terms.name: FILE CONTROL
terms.longDescription: FILE CONTROL is the set of CICS commands to access VSAM files. It allows reading, writing, updating, and deleting records transactionally.
terms.examples: EXEC CICS READ FILE('CLIENTES') INTO(WS-REG) END-EXEC
terms.notes: Requires FILE definition in the CSD.

terms.name: READ FILE
terms.longDescription: READ FILE allows reading a VSAM record from CICS. It can be performed by key or by position, depending on the file type.
terms.examples: EXEC CICS READ FILE('CLIENTES') RIDFLD(WS-CLAVE) INTO(WS-REG) END-EXEC
terms.notes: NOTFND must be handled for non-existent keys.

terms.name: WRITE FILE
terms.longDescription: WRITE FILE inserts a new record into a VSAM file. It is transactional and requires SYNCPOINT for confirmation.
terms.examples: EXEC CICS WRITE FILE('CLIENTES') FROM(WS-REG) END-EXEC
terms.notes: May fail if the key already exists.

terms.name: REWRITE FILE
terms.longDescription: REWRITE FILE updates a record previously read with READ UPDATE. It maintains file integrity and is part of transactional control.
terms.examples: EXEC CICS REWRITE FILE('CLIENTES') FROM(WS-REG) END-EXEC
terms.notes: Requires a prior READ UPDATE.

terms.name: DELETE FILE
terms.longDescription: DELETE FILE deletes a VSAM record identified by key. It is useful for data maintenance or administrative processes.
terms.examples: EXEC CICS DELETE FILE('CLIENTES') RIDFLD(WS-CLAVE) END-EXEC
terms.notes: NOTFND must be handled if the key does not exist.

terms.name: START
terms.longDescription: START allows initiating a transaction in the background or deferred, passing optional parameters via COMMAREA. It is useful for asynchronous processes.
terms.examples: EXEC CICS START TRANSID('B001') COMMAREA(WS-DATOS) END-EXEC
terms.notes: The initiated transaction does not return control to the current program.

terms.name: SELECT
terms.longDescription: SELECT is the primary statement to retrieve data from a table or view in DB2. It allows specifying columns, filters, sorting, and aggregate functions. It is the basis of any read operation in SQL.
terms.notes: Can be combined with JOIN, GROUP BY, HAVING, and ORDER BY.

terms.name: INSERT
terms.shortDescription: Inserts a record into a table
terms.longDescription: INSERT adds new records to a table. It can specify all columns or only some, provided the remaining ones have default values or allow NULL.
terms.notes: Requires COMMIT to persist changes.

terms.name: UPDATE
terms.longDescription: UPDATE modifies column values in existing records. It must be used with WHERE to avoid accidentally updating the entire table.
terms.examples: UPDATE CLIENTES SET ESTADO = 'I' WHERE ID = 100;
terms.notes: Without WHERE, it updates all records.

terms.name: DELETE
terms.longDescription: DELETE removes records from a table based on a condition. It is a transactional operation that requires COMMIT to be confirmed.
terms.notes: Without WHERE, it deletes all records.

terms.name: COMMIT
terms.longDescription: COMMIT confirms all changes made in the current transaction, making INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE operations permanent.
terms.notes: In CICS, SYNCPOINT performs the same function.

terms.name: ROLLBACK
terms.longDescription: ROLLBACK reverts all changes made since the last COMMIT. It is essential for handling errors and maintaining data integrity.
terms.notes: In CICS, ROLLBACK performs the same function.

terms.name: DECLARE CURSOR
terms.shortDescription: Defines a cursor to traverse results
terms.longDescription: DECLARE CURSOR defines a cursor that allows traversing row by row the result of a query. It is fundamental in COBOL programs with embedded SQL.
terms.examples: DECLARE C1 CURSOR FOR SELECT ID, NOMBRE FROM CLIENTES;
terms.notes: Must be opened with OPEN and closed with CLOSE.

terms.name: OPEN CURSOR
terms.longDescription: OPEN CURSOR executes the query associated with the cursor and leaves it ready to perform FETCH.
terms.notes: If the query fails, SQLCODE will contain the error.

terms.name: FETCH
terms.longDescription: FETCH retrieves the next row from the cursor and stores it in host variables. It allows traversing sequential results.
terms.notes: SQLCODE = +100 indicates end of data.

terms.name: CLOSE CURSOR
terms.longDescription: CLOSE CURSOR releases the resources associated with the cursor. It is mandatory to prevent memory leaks or locks.
terms.notes: Must always be executed, even if errors occurred.

terms.name: WHERE
terms.longDescription: WHERE allows filtering records based on logical conditions. It is essential for precise and efficient queries.
terms.notes: Can be combined with AND, OR, and relational operators.

terms.name: GROUP BY
terms.longDescription: GROUP BY groups records according to one or more columns, allowing aggregate functions like SUM, COUNT, or AVG to be applied.
terms.examples: SELECT ESTADO, COUNT(*) FROM CLIENTES GROUP BY ESTADO;
terms.notes: Non-aggregated columns must appear in GROUP BY.

terms.name: HAVING
terms.longDescription: HAVING filters results after applying GROUP BY. It allows conditions on aggregates.
terms.examples: SELECT ESTADO, COUNT(*) FROM CLIENTES GROUP BY ESTADO HAVING COUNT(*) > 10;
terms.notes: WHERE filters rows; HAVING filters groups.

terms.name: ORDER BY
terms.longDescription: ORDER BY sorts the results based on one or more columns, in ascending or descending order.
terms.examples: SELECT * FROM CLIENTES ORDER BY NOMBRE ASC;
terms.notes: Can sort by unselected columns.

terms.name: JOIN
terms.longDescription: JOIN allows combining records from two or more tables based on a defined relationship. It is essential for complex relational queries.
terms.examples: SELECT C.NOMBRE, P.SALDO FROM CLIENTES C JOIN CUENTAS P ON C.ID = P.ID_CLIENTE;
terms.notes: JOIN without an explicit type defaults to INNER JOIN.

terms.name: INNER JOIN
terms.longDescription: INNER JOIN returns only records that have matches in both tables. It is the most common type of JOIN.
terms.examples: SELECT * FROM A INNER JOIN B ON A.ID = B.ID;
terms.notes: Unmatched records do not appear.

terms.name: LEFT JOIN
terms.shortDescription: Returns all records from the left table
terms.longDescription: LEFT JOIN returns all records from the left table, even if they have no match in the right table.
terms.examples: SELECT * FROM A LEFT JOIN B ON A.ID = B.ID;
terms.notes: Unmatched values appear as NULL.

terms.name: RIGHT JOIN
terms.shortDescription: Returns all records from the right table
terms.longDescription: RIGHT JOIN returns all records from the right table, even if they have no match in the left table.
terms.examples: SELECT * FROM A RIGHT JOIN B ON A.ID = B.ID;
terms.notes: Less used than LEFT JOIN.

terms.name: FULL JOIN
terms.shortDescription: Returns all records from both tables
terms.longDescription: FULL JOIN returns all records from both tables, including matches and non-matches.
terms.examples: SELECT * FROM A FULL JOIN B ON A.ID = B.ID;
terms.notes: Unmatched records show NULL in the opposite table.

terms.name: UNION
terms.longDescription: UNION combines results from two queries and automatically removes duplicates.
terms.examples: SELECT ID FROM A UNION SELECT ID FROM B;
terms.notes: Columns must be compatible in type and quantity.

terms.name: UNION ALL
terms.longDescription: UNION ALL combines results from two queries without removing duplicates. It is faster than UNION.
terms.examples: SELECT ID FROM A UNION ALL SELECT ID FROM B;
terms.notes: Ideal for large volumes of data.

terms.name: PRIMARY KEY
terms.longDescription: PRIMARY KEY defines a column or set of columns that uniquely identify each record in a table.
terms.notes: Does not allow NULL values.

terms.name: FOREIGN KEY
terms.longDescription: FOREIGN KEY establishes a relationship between tables, guaranteeing referential integrity.
terms.notes: May require indexes to improve performance.

terms.name: INDEX
terms.longDescription: An INDEX speeds up searches and sorting by creating optimized structures based on key columns.
terms.notes: Too many indexes can affect INSERT/UPDATE performance.

terms.name: TABLESPACE
terms.longDescription: TABLESPACE defines the physical space where tables and indexes are stored. It allows managing storage and performance.
terms.notes: Can be partitioned for large volumes.

terms.name: BUFFERPOOL
terms.longDescription: BUFFERPOOL is allocated memory used to store data and index pages, improving access performance.
terms.notes: A well-sized bufferpool improves response times.

terms.name: PLAN
terms.longDescription: A PLAN is the executable object containing one or more packages. It is used by programs to interact with DB2.
terms.notes: In modern environments, PACKAGE is used more than PLAN.

terms.name: PACKAGE
terms.longDescription: A PACKAGE contains compiled and optimized SQL code. It is the basic unit of execution in DB2.
terms.notes: Packages are grouped into plans.

terms.name: BIND
terms.longDescription: BIND compiles and optimizes embedded SQL in programs, generating packages or plans according to configuration.
terms.notes: The BIND determines the access path.

terms.name: REBIND
terms.longDescription: REBIND recompiles an existing package to update statistics or improve performance.
terms.notes: Useful after RUNSTATS or index changes.

terms.name: RUNSTATS
terms.longDescription: RUNSTATS updates statistics for tables and indexes, allowing the optimizer to generate better access paths.
terms.notes: Must be run regularly in production.

terms.name: REORG
terms.longDescription: REORG physically reorganizes tables and indexes to improve performance by eliminating fragmentation.
terms.notes: Recommended after large DELETE operations.

terms.name: LOAD
terms.longDescription: LOAD allows loading large volumes of data into a table efficiently, avoiding INSERT overhead.
terms.examples: LOAD DATA INDDN(INPUT) INTO TABLE CLIENTES;
terms.notes: May require a subsequent REORG.

terms.name: UNLOAD
terms.longDescription: UNLOAD extracts large volumes of data from a table to an external dataset.
terms.notes: Ideal for migrations or backups.

terms.name: LOCK
terms.longDescription: LOCK controls concurrent access to tables and rows, preventing inconsistencies during updates.
terms.notes: Excessive locking can cause deadlocks.

terms.name: DEADLOCK
terms.longDescription: A deadlock occurs when two or more transactions block each other while waiting for resources held by the other. DB2 automatically detects the situation and cancels one of the transactions to release the lock and allow the system to continue functioning.
terms.examples: SQLCODE -911 indicates a deadlock detected by DB2.
terms.notes: It is recommended to review indexes and access order to prevent deadlocks.

terms.name: ISOLATION LEVEL
terms.longDescription: The isolation level determines how a transaction views changes made by other transactions. It controls phenomena such as dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, and phantom reads. DB2 supports various levels that balance consistency and performance.
terms.notes: Stricter levels reduce concurrency but increase consistency.

terms.name: WITH UR
terms.longDescription: WITH UR allows reading data not yet committed by other transactions. It is the lowest isolation level and offers maximum performance, but it may return inconsistent data.
terms.notes: Ideal for read-only queries on very large tables.

terms.name: WITH CS
terms.longDescription: WITH CS ensures that data read by the cursor does not change while the row is being processed. It prevents dirty reads but allows non-repeatable reads.
terms.notes: This is the default level in many installations.

terms.name: WITH RS
terms.longDescription: WITH RS ensures that rows read do not change during the transaction. It prevents non-repeatable reads, but allows phantom reads.
terms.notes: Suitable for processes requiring data stability.

terms.name: WITH RR
terms.longDescription: WITH RR is the strictest isolation level. It guarantees that data does not change throughout the entire transaction and prevents all concurrency phenomena, including phantom reads.
terms.notes: Significantly reduces concurrency; use only when necessary.

terms.name: EXPLAIN
terms.longDescription: EXPLAIN retrieves the execution plan that DB2 will use for an SQL statement. It is essential for query optimization and performance analysis.
terms.examples: EXPLAIN PLAN FOR SELECT * FROM CLIENTES;
terms.notes: Results are stored in special tables within the PLAN_TABLE schema.

terms.name: SQLCODE
terms.longDescription: SQLCODE is the numeric code indicating the result of an SQL statement. Positive values indicate warnings, zero indicates success, and negative values indicate errors.
terms.notes: Must be checked after each SQL statement in COBOL programs.

terms.name: SQLSTATE
terms.longDescription: SQLSTATE is a five-character code indicating the status of an SQL operation following ANSI standards. It provides more portable information than SQLCODE.
terms.notes: Useful for multi-platform applications.

terms.name: HOST VARIABLES
terms.longDescription: Host variables are COBOL variables used to send and receive data from embedded SQL statements. They are identified by the ':' prefix in statements.
terms.examples: SELECT NOMBRE INTO :WS-NOMBRE FROM CLIENTES WHERE ID = :WS-ID;
terms.notes: Must be declared in WORKING-STORAGE.

terms.name: DECLARE TABLE
terms.longDescription: DECLARE TABLE allows defining temporary tables within programs to manipulate data without affecting real tables. It is mainly used in dynamic SQL.
terms.examples: DECLARE GLOBAL TEMPORARY TABLE SESSION.TMP AS (SELECT * FROM CLIENTES) WITH DATA;
terms.notes: Temporary tables exist only during the session.

terms.name: GLOBAL TEMPORARY TABLE
terms.longDescription: A GLOBAL TEMPORARY TABLE is a temporary table that exists solely during the user's session. It allows storing intermediate data without affecting permanent tables.
terms.examples: DECLARE GLOBAL TEMPORARY TABLE SESSION.TMP_CLIENTES (ID INT, NOMBRE VARCHAR(50));
terms.notes: Data is automatically deleted when the session ends.

terms.name: VIEW
terms.longDescription: A VIEW is a logical table based on a query. It simplifies data access, hides complexity, and improves security.
terms.examples: CREATE VIEW V_CLIENTES_ACTIVOS AS SELECT * FROM CLIENTES WHERE ESTADO = 'A';
terms.notes: Views do not store data; they depend on the base tables.

terms.name: ALIAS
terms.longDescription: An ALIAS is an alternative name for a table or view. It facilitates access to objects in other schemas or databases.
terms.notes: Does not affect permissions or structure.

terms.name: SEQUENCE
terms.longDescription: A SEQUENCE is an object that generates sequential or incremental numeric values. It is used for primary keys or unique identifiers.
terms.examples: CREATE SEQUENCE SEQ_CLIENTE START WITH 1 INCREMENT BY 1;
terms.notes: Can be used with NEXT VALUE FOR in INSERT statements.

terms.name: ABORT
terms.longDescription: ABORT ends program execution without performing additional cleanup or executing termination blocks. It is used to halt execution when a critical condition prevents continuation.
terms.notes: Interrupts normal flow and does not guarantee resource release.

terms.name: ABSENT
terms.shortDescription: Indicates the absence of a value in lists or optional parameters.
terms.longDescription: ABSENT is used to signal that an optional parameter or list element is not present. It distinguishes between null values and explicit absence.
terms.examples: IF ARGUMENT(3) = ABSENT THEN CALL HANDLE_MISSING();
terms.notes: Useful in routines with optional parameters to validate presence.

terms.name: ACCESS
terms.shortDescription: Specifies access mode for a file or resource.
terms.longDescription: ACCESS defines how a file will be opened or used, indicating whether access will be sequential, direct, read, or write. It controls the behavior of I/O operations.
terms.notes: Must be consistent with the file type and intended operations.

terms.name: ACCEPT
terms.shortDescription: Accepts input or confirms a value.
terms.longDescription: ACCEPT is used to receive data from an input device or to confirm values in certain contexts. Its exact behavior depends on the execution environment.
terms.notes: May vary depending on the system implementation.

terms.name: ACOS
terms.longDescription: ACOS returns the angle whose cosine is the provided value. It is used in mathematical calculations requiring the conversion of trigonometric values to angles.
terms.notes: The argument must be within the valid range for cosine.

terms.name: ADDRESS
terms.shortDescription: Returns or declares the memory address of a variable.
terms.longDescription: ADDRESS retrieves the physical location of an object in memory or declares variables based on specific addresses. It is fundamental for pointer manipulation.
terms.notes: Must be used with caution to avoid invalid memory access.

terms.name: ALIGN
terms.shortDescription: Aligns data in memory according to implementation requirements.
terms.longDescription: ALIGN specifies that a variable must be located in memory respecting alignment boundaries. This improves performance and prevents failures on architectures that require it.
terms.notes: Alignment depends on the hardware and the compiler.

terms.name: ALLOCATE
terms.longDescription: ALLOCATE creates dynamic space for variables or structures during execution. It is essential for managing flexible memory and variable-sized structures.
terms.notes: Must be complemented with DEALLOCATE to prevent memory leaks.

terms.name: AND
terms.longDescription: AND evaluates two conditions and returns true only if both are true. It is used in logical expressions within control structures.
terms.notes: Evaluates both operands barring compiler optimizations.

terms.name: ANY
terms.shortDescription: Type or clause that accepts any data type.
terms.longDescription: ANY allows declaring parameters or elements that can receive values of any compatible type. It facilitates the creation of generic routines.
terms.notes: Must be used with validations to avoid type errors.

terms.name: APPEND
terms.shortDescription: Appends data to the end of a file or list.
terms.longDescription: APPEND is used to add new elements to the end of a sequential structure, whether a file or a list. It allows extending content without modifying existing elements.
terms.notes: The file access mode must allow sequential writing.

terms.name: ARGUMENT
terms.shortDescription: References a parameter passed to a routine.
terms.longDescription: ARGUMENT provides access to parameters received by a routine, especially when working with argument lists or optional parameters. It facilitates dynamic inspection of values.
terms.examples: IF ARGUMENT(2) = ABSENT THEN CALL HANDLE();
terms.notes: Useful in generic procedures with a variable number of parameters.

terms.name: ARRAY
terms.shortDescription: Declares an indexed collection of elements.
terms.longDescription: ARRAY defines an ordered set of elements accessible via indices. It is fundamental for managing structured data and collections of fixed or variable size.
terms.notes: Array bounds can be static or dynamic depending on the declaration.

terms.name: AS
terms.longDescription: AS is used to establish equivalences or aliases between names, allowing a variable or structure to adopt the type or format of another declaration.
terms.notes: Facilitates reusing definitions without duplicating structures.

terms.name: ASSERT
terms.longDescription: ASSERT verifies that a condition is true during execution. If it fails, it can trigger diagnostic mechanisms or stop the program depending on configuration.
terms.notes: Useful for debugging and invariant validation.

terms.name: ASSIGN
terms.shortDescription: Assigns values or reassigns external names; also for files.
terms.longDescription: ASSIGN associates external files with logical names or sets values in variables. It is key for configuring resources prior to I/O operations.
terms.notes: Must be executed before opening the file to take effect.

terms.name: ATAN
terms.longDescription: ATAN returns the angle whose tangent corresponds to the provided value. It is used in mathematical calculations requiring the conversion of trigonometric ratios into angles.
terms.notes: The result is in radians.

terms.name: ATAN2
terms.longDescription: ATAN2 calculates the angle considering two values, allowing determination of the correct quadrant. It is useful in vector and coordinate operations.
terms.notes: Avoids sign ambiguities present in ATAN.

terms.name: AUTO
terms.longDescription: AUTO indicates that a variable is created upon entering a block and destroyed upon exit. It is the typical storage class for local variables.
terms.notes: Its lifetime depends strictly on the block where it is declared.

terms.name: AUTO_DEALLOCATE
terms.shortDescription: Automatically frees storage upon exiting the block.
terms.longDescription: AUTO_DEALLOCATE ensures that dynamically allocated storage is released when the block finishes. It simplifies memory management in temporary structures.
terms.notes: Prevents memory leaks in routines with repeated allocations.

terms.name: BASED
terms.shortDescription: Defines data whose content is located at an address.
terms.longDescription: BASED allows declaring variables that rely on a pointer to determine their memory location. It is essential for manipulating dynamic structures.
terms.notes: A valid address must be assigned before using the based variable.

terms.name: BINARY
terms.shortDescription: Type or mode indicating binary representation.
terms.longDescription: BINARY specifies that a numeric value is stored in binary format. It is common in arithmetic operations and fixed-precision calculations.
terms.notes: Precision depends on the declared number of bits.

terms.name: BIT
terms.shortDescription: Bit data type or bitwise manipulations.
terms.longDescription: BIT allows declaring variables that represent bit sequences. It is useful for mask operations, flags, and compact field manipulation.
terms.notes: Bitwise operations depend on the declared size.

terms.name: BLOCK
terms.shortDescription: Groups instructions into a structured block.
terms.longDescription: BLOCK defines a section of code with its own scope for variables and flow control. It facilitates the logical organization of the program.
terms.notes: Allows declaring variables local to the block.

terms.name: BOOLEAN
terms.longDescription: BOOLEAN represents logical values used in conditions and control expressions. It is fundamental for IF, WHILE, and CASE structures.
terms.notes: Its internal representation depends on the compiler.

terms.name: BUILTIN
terms.shortDescription: Identifies a compiler-provided function or routine.
terms.longDescription: BUILTIN marks functions provided directly by the compiler, optimized for performance and available without explicit definition.
terms.notes: Builtin functions may vary across implementations.

terms.name: BY
terms.longDescription: BY is used to specify increments in loops or to define separation in I/O operations. It controls the progression of iterations.
terms.notes: The BY value can be positive or negative depending on the loop direction.

terms.name: CALL
terms.longDescription: CALL executes a previously defined routine, passing the necessary arguments. It is the main mechanism for modularizing programs.
terms.notes: Parameters must match the procedure definition.

terms.name: CASE
terms.longDescription: CASE allows choosing between multiple branches based on the value of an expression. It simplifies complex decisions with multiple alternatives.
terms.examples: SELECT (X); WHEN(1) CALL A; WHEN(2) CALL B; END;
terms.notes: Must include a branch for unpredicted values if robustness is required.

terms.name: CEILING
terms.longDescription: CEILING returns the smallest integer greater than or equal to the provided value. It is used in calculations requiring values to be adjusted upward.
terms.notes: The result is always an integer.

terms.name: CHAR
terms.longDescription: CHAR declares fixed-length strings stored with the exact specified size. It is used to represent structured text, input fields, and alphanumeric data.
terms.notes: CHAR strings are padded with spaces if the content is shorter than the declared length.

terms.name: CHECK
terms.longDescription: CHECK triggers runtime or compilation checks depending on the context. It allows detecting anomalous conditions and validating behaviors during execution.
terms.notes: Its effect depends on compilation options and the environment.

terms.name: CLASS
